claim: 74% (70–78%, 95% posterior interval) of SARS-CoV-2 infections on the Diamond Princess proceeded asymptomatically.
source: The model estimated that 74% (70–78%, 95% posterior interval) of infections proceeded asymptomatically.
evidence: The claim is supported by model estimates calibrated to data from the Diamond Princess outbreak, including disease onset dates and test frequency.

claim: 53% (51–56%) of infections on the Diamond Princess remained undetected despite intense testing.
source: Despite intense testing, 53% (51–56%) of infections remained undetected, most of them asymptomatic.
evidence: The claim is based on model estimates using data from the Diamond Princess outbreak.

claim: Most undetected infections on the Diamond Princess were asymptomatic.
source: Despite intense testing, 53% (51–56%) of infections remained undetected, most of them asymptomatic.
evidence: The claim is supported by model estimates analyzing detected versus undetected infections.

claim: Asymptomatic individuals were the source for 69% (20–85%) of all infections on the Diamond Princess.
source: Asymptomatic individuals were the source for 69% (20–85%) of all infections.
evidence: The claim is based on model estimates of transmission contributions from different infection states.

claim: Low relative infectiousness of asymptomatic infections (0–25%) would require a net reproduction number for presymptomatic and symptomatic individuals of at least 15.
source: The data did not allow identification of the infectiousness of asymptomatic infections, however low ranges (0–25%) required a net reproduction number for individuals progressing through presymptomatic and symptomatic stages of at least 15.
evidence: The claim is based on model inference exploring trade-offs between relative infectiousness and reproduction numbers.

claim: The data from the Diamond Princess did not allow identification of the infectiousness of asymptomatic infections.
source: The data did not allow identification of the infectiousness of asymptomatic infections, however low ranges (0–25%) required a net reproduction number for individuals progressing through presymptomatic and symptomatic stages of at least 15.
evidence: The claim is based on the inability of the model to identify this parameter from the available data.

claim: Asymptomatic SARS-CoV-2 infections may contribute substantially to transmission.
source: Asymptomatic SARS-CoV-2 infections may contribute substantially to transmission.
evidence: The claim is supported by model estimates showing high contribution of asymptomatic infections to overall transmission.

claim: Control measures need to look beyond symptomatic cases to understand and address ongoing SARS-CoV-2 transmission.
source: Control measures, and models projecting their potential impact, need to look beyond the symptomatic cases if they are to understand and address ongoing transmission.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the finding that asymptomatic infections contribute substantially to transmission.

claim: The number of individuals infected with SARS-CoV-2 outstrips the number of reported cases.
source: The ongoing COVID-19 pandemic has spread rapidly across the globe, and the number of individuals infected with SARS-CoV-2 outstrips the number of reported cases (Wang et al., 2020; Golding et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to other studies.

claim: A substantial proportion of SARS-CoV-2 cases proceed asymptomatically.
source: One key reason for this may be that a substantial proportion of cases proceed asymptomatically, that is, they either do not experience or are not aware of symptoms throughout their infection but may still transmit to others.
evidence: The claim is presented as a hypothesis to explain why infections outnumber reported cases.

claim: Asymptomatic infections differ from presymptomatic infections in that asymptomatic individuals do not experience or are not aware of symptoms throughout their infection.
source: In this sense, asymptomatic infections differ from presymptomatic infections, which describes the portion of the incubation period before symptoms develop during which onward transmission is possible.
evidence: The claim is a definitional statement based on established understanding of disease states.

claim: Presymptomatic infections describe the portion of the incubation period before symptoms develop during which onward transmission is possible.
source: In this sense, asymptomatic infections differ from presymptomatic infections, which describes the portion of the incubation period before symptoms develop during which onward transmission is possible.
evidence: The claim is a definitional statement based on established understanding of disease states.

claim: Pre- and asymptomatic individuals can contribute to ongoing SARS-CoV-2 transmission.
source: While pre- and asymptomatic individuals do not directly contribute to morbidity or mortality in an outbreak, they can contribute to ongoing transmission, as has been shown for COVID-19 (Rothe et al., 2020; Chen et al., 2020; Ganyani et al., 2020) and other diseases (Dean et al., 2016; Slater et al., 2019; Esmail et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies on COVID-19 and other diseases.

claim: Purely symptom-based interventions will not interrupt transmission from asymptomatic individuals.
source: In particular, purely symptom-based interventions (e.g., self-isolation upon onset of disease) will not interrupt transmission from asymptomatic individuals and hence may be insufficient for outbreak control if a substantial proportion of transmission originates from pre- and asymptomatic infections (Chen et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is a logical inference about the limitations of symptom-based interventions, supported by citation.

claim: Symptom-based interventions may be insufficient for outbreak control if a substantial proportion of transmission originates from pre- and asymptomatic infections.
source: In particular, purely symptom-based interventions (e.g., self-isolation upon onset of disease) will not interrupt transmission from asymptomatic individuals and hence may be insufficient for outbreak control if a substantial proportion of transmission originates from pre- and asymptomatic infections (Chen et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is a logical inference supported by citation.

claim: The proportion of SARS-CoV-2 infections that proceed asymptomatically is likely non-trivial.
source: Evidence so far have suggested that the proportion of SARS-CoV-2 infections that proceed asymptomatically is likely non-trivial (Li et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2020a; He et al., 2020; Mizumoto et al., 2020; Lavezzo et al., 2020; Bendavid et al., 2020), although empirical data are often difficult to interpret due to opportunistic sampling frames (Nishiura et al., 2020) combined with low (Fontanet et al., 2020) and imbalanced participation from individuals with and without symptoms (Gudbjartsson et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to studies on asymptomatic infections.

claim: Empirical data on asymptomatic SARS-CoV-2 infections are often difficult to interpret due to opportunistic sampling frames combined with low and imbalanced participation from individuals with and without symptoms.
source: Evidence so far have suggested that the proportion of SARS-CoV-2 infections that proceed asymptomatically is likely non-trivial (Li et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2020a; He et al., 2020; Mizumoto et al., 2020; Lavezzo et al., 2020; Bendavid et al., 2020), although empirical data are often difficult to interpret due to opportunistic sampling frames (Nishiura et al., 2020) combined with low (Fontanet et al., 2020) and imbalanced participation from individuals with and without symptoms (Gudbjartsson et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies discussing methodological challenges.

claim: Transmission from asymptomatic SARS-CoV-2 individuals can occur.
source: While it is likely that transmission from asymptomatic individuals can occur, (Bai et al., 2020) quantitative estimates are effectively absent.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a study.

claim: Quantitative estimates of transmission from asymptomatic SARS-CoV-2 individuals are effectively absent.
source: While it is likely that transmission from asymptomatic individuals can occur, (Bai et al., 2020) quantitative estimates are effectively absent.
evidence: The claim is an assessment of the state of evidence in the literature.

claim: In the presence of active case-finding, presymptomatic infections and symptomatic cases contribute almost equally to overall SARS-CoV-2 transmission.
source: What is known is that in the presence of active case-finding, presymptomatic infections and symptomatic cases contribute almost equally to overall transmission, as both modelling and empirical studies have shown (Liu et al., 2020a; He et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to modeling and empirical studies.

claim: The model reflected the data well, including the differently timed peaks for confirmed symptomatic cases for crew and passengers.
source: The model reflected the data well (Figure 1), including the differently timed peaks for confirmed symptomatic cases for crew (Figure 1A) and passengers (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of model outputs to data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The model matched the expected impact of quarantine of passengers on transmission from February 4th as illustrated by the drop in reproductive number.
source: In addition, the model matched the expected impact of quarantine of passengers on transmission from February 4th as illustrated by the drop in reproductive number (Figure 1E), followed by a later drop in transmission after February 10th, which was driven by a change in contact pattern in crew.
evidence: The claim is supported by model outputs shown in Figure 1E.

claim: A drop in transmission after February 10th was driven by a change in contact pattern in crew.
source: In addition, the model matched the expected impact of quarantine of passengers on transmission from February 4th as illustrated by the drop in reproductive number (Figure 1E), followed by a later drop in transmission after February 10th, which was driven by a change in contact pattern in crew.
evidence: The claim is based on model inference about the cause of the observed drop in transmission.

claim: In total 1304 (1,198–1,416) individuals were infected on the Diamond Princess.
source: As a result, our model estimated that in total 1304 (1,198–1,416) individuals were infected, representing 35% (32–38%) of the initial total population on the Diamond Princess.
evidence: The claim is based on model estimates.

claim: 35% (32–38%) of the initial total population on the Diamond Princess were infected.
source: As a result, our model estimated that in total 1304 (1,198–1,416) individuals were infected, representing 35% (32–38%) of the initial total population on the Diamond Princess.
evidence: The claim is based on model estimates.

claim: Over half of infections on the Diamond Princess had not been detected at disembarkation on February 21st (53%, 51–56%).
source: Over half of these infections had not been detected at disembarkation on February 21 st (53%, 51–56%) consisting of infected individuals who had recovered and became test negative before they were tested (37%, 34–40%), were yet to be tested (15%, 13–16%), or had recently been exposed and were not yet detectable at that point (1%, 1–3%).
evidence: The claim is based on model estimates.

claim: 37% (34–40%) of infections on the Diamond Princess consisted of individuals who had recovered and became test negative before they were tested.
source: Over half of these infections had not been detected at disembarkation on February 21 st (53%, 51–56%) consisting of infected individuals who had recovered and became test negative before they were tested (37%, 34–40%), were yet to be tested (15%, 13–16%), or had recently been exposed and were not yet detectable at that point (1%, 1–3%).
evidence: The claim is based on model estimates.

claim: 15% (13–16%) of infections on the Diamond Princess were yet to be tested at disembarkation.
source: Over half of these infections had not been detected at disembarkation on February 21 st (53%, 51–56%) consisting of infected individuals who had recovered and became test negative before they were tested (37%, 34–40%), were yet to be tested (15%, 13–16%), or had recently been exposed and were not yet detectable at that point (1%, 1–3%).
evidence: The claim is based on model estimates.

claim: 1% (1–3%) of infections on the Diamond Princess had recently been exposed and were not yet detectable at disembarkation.
source: Over half of these infections had not been detected at disembarkation on February 21 st (53%, 51–56%) consisting of infected individuals who had recovered and became test negative before they were tested (37%, 34–40%), were yet to be tested (15%, 13–16%), or had recently been exposed and were not yet detectable at that point (1%, 1–3%).
evidence: The claim is based on model estimates.

claim: Nearly two-thirds of pre- and asymptomatic infections (67%, 66–68%) went undetected up until disembarkation.
source: Nearly two-thirds of pre- and asymptomatic infections (67%, 66–68%) and 8% (6–9%) of symptomatic infections went undetected up until disembarkation (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is based on model estimates shown in Figure 2C.

claim: 8% (6–9%) of symptomatic infections went undetected up until disembarkation.
source: Nearly two-thirds of pre- and asymptomatic infections (67%, 66–68%) and 8% (6–9%) of symptomatic infections went undetected up until disembarkation (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is based on model estimates shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The model was unable to identify the relative infectiousness of asymptomatic infections from the data.
source: In contrast to the strong identifiability of the proportion of infections that were asymptomatic, the model was unable to identify the relative infectiousness of asymptomatic infections from the data, that is, a uniform prior was effectively returned (see Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is based on model calibration results shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The relative infectiousness of asymptomatic infections was degenerate with the overall contact rate.
source: This is because the relative infectiousness of asymptomatic infections was degenerate with the overall contact rate, meaning the data were consistent with either relatively frequent contact with less infectious individuals or relatively infrequent contact with more infectious individuals (see Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is based on model analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The estimated proportion of transmission due to asymptomatic infections is 69%, with a wide confidence interval (20–85%) and an interquartile range of 56–76%.
source: Despite this, the estimated proportion of transmission due to asymptomatic infections is 69%, with a wide confidence interval (20–85%) and an interquartile range of 56–76% (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is based on model estimates shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Only a modest relative infectiousness is required to produce a non-trivial contribution to transmission from asymptomatic infections.
source: The result is that only a modest relative infectiousness is required to produce a non-trivial contribution to transmission.
evidence: The claim is based on model analysis of the relationship between relative infectiousness and contribution to transmission.

claim: The relative infectiousness of presymptomatics was unidentifiable.
source: The relative infectiousness of presymptomatics was also unidentifiable, however, in all scenarios the remaining transmission was equally distributed between the presymptomatic (14%, 1–44%) and symptomatic (17%, 11–42%) individuals.
evidence: The claim is based on model calibration results.

claim: In all scenarios the remaining transmission was equally distributed between the presymptomatic (14%, 1–44%) and symptomatic (17%, 11–42%) individuals.
source: The relative infectiousness of presymptomatics was also unidentifiable, however, in all scenarios the remaining transmission was equally distributed between the presymptomatic (14%, 1–44%) and symptomatic (17%, 11–42%) individuals.
evidence: The claim is based on model estimates.

claim: Low relative infectiousness of asymptomatic infections (0–25% compared to symptomatic individuals) would need to be compensated by a net reproduction number for individuals during their presymptomatic and symptomatic phase of 15.5–29.1.
source: We find that low relative infectiousness of asymptomatic infections (0–25% compared to symptomatic individuals) would need to be compensated by a net reproduction number for individuals during their presymptomatic and symptomatic phase of 15.5–29.1.
evidence: The claim is based on model analysis of marginal posterior estimates shown in Table 1.

claim: Without an asymptomatic state the model was unable to reconstruct the dynamics of the outbreak.
source: Without an asymptomatic state the model was unable to reconstruct the dynamics of the outbreak (Appendix 2—figures 1–3, Deviance Information Criterion (DIC) = 974 vs 329 for the primary analysis).
evidence: The claim is based on sensitivity analysis comparing model fit with and without asymptomatic state.

claim: Adjusting the relative value for mixing between crew and passengers did not have a qualitative effect on the results.
source: Moreover, adjusting the relative value for mixing between crew and passengers did not have a qualitative effect on the results (Appendix 2—figures 4–11).
evidence: The claim is based on sensitivity analysis.

claim: Biased symptom-agnostic testing had a greater impact on the results than adjusting mixing between crew and passengers.
source: Biased symptom-agnostic testing had a greater impact on the results.
evidence: The claim is based on sensitivity analysis comparing different scenarios.

claim: When those testing negative had a 50% higher probability of being tested, the proportion of infections that were asymptomatic was 84% (82–87%).
source: Those testing negative having a 50% higher probability of being tested compared to the primary analysis led to a corresponding greater proportion of infections that were asymptomatic (84%, 82–87%), total number infected (2,097, 1,914-2,292) and contribution of asymptomatics to transmission (78%, 36–91%) (see Appendix 2—figures 12–15).
evidence: The claim is based on sensitivity analysis.

claim: When those testing positive had a 50% higher probability of being tested, the proportion of infections that were asymptomatic was 66% (61–71%).
source: Conversely, those testing positive having a 50% higher probability of being tested compared to the primary analysis led to a corresponding smaller proportion of infections that were asymptomatic (66%, 61–71%), total number infected (1,051, 965-1,161) and contribution of asymptomatics to transmission (59%, 9–79%) (see Appendix 2—figures 16–19).
evidence: The claim is based on sensitivity analysis.

claim: When assuming a fixed age-specific ratio for the proportion of infections that progress asymptomatically, the proportion asymptomatic was 42% (41–44%) for passengers and 89% (85–91%) for crew.
source: When we assumed a fixed age-specific ratio for the proportion of infections that progress asymptomatically, the model was able to fit the data, although the number of correlated parameters was high. Overall results were similar to the main analysis, with a proportion asymptomatic of 42% (41–44%) and 89% (85–91%) for passengers and crew, respectively.
evidence: The claim is based on sensitivity analysis with age-specific assumptions.

claim: A longer latent period provided a poorer fit to the data (DIC = 361).
source: A longer latent period provided a poorer fit to the data (DIC = 361) (Appendix 2—figures 24–27).
evidence: The claim is based on sensitivity analysis comparing model fit.

claim: Adjusting the duration of the asymptomatic state to half or double the sum of the presymptomatic and symptomatic states made little qualitative difference to the results.
source: Adjusting the duration of the asymptomatic state to half or double the sum of the presymptomatic and symptomatic states made little qualitative difference to the results (Appendix 2—figures 28–35), although the shorter asymptomatic period was a marginally poorer fit to the data (DIC = 338).
evidence: The claim is based on sensitivity analysis.

claim: The estimated proportion of asymptomatic infections in this outbreak is higher than previous studies which relied on diagnosed cases only.
source: Our estimated proportion of asymptomatic infections in this outbreak is higher than previous studies, which relied on diagnosed cases only (Mizumoto et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim compares the current study's results to previous studies, supported by citation.

claim: A substantial number of infections were not detected on the Diamond Princess, which would explain some of the difference from previous studies.
source: As we have shown, a substantial number of infections were not detected, which would explain some of the difference.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the study's findings.

claim: It is possible that PCR-based testing has a lower sensitivity for asymptomatic individuals.
source: In addition, it is possible that PCR-based testing has a lower sensitivity for asymptomatic individuals, which would further increase the proportion of infections that were asymptomatic (Chau et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is a speculation supported by citation.

claim: The results were robust to age-specific probabilities of progressing to asymptomatic infections.
source: A sensitivity analysis showed that our results were robust to age-specific probabilities of progressing to asymptomatic infections, as well as other assumptions made in the model, and driven by trends in the data.
evidence: The claim is based on sensitivity analysis.

claim: The estimated substantial contribution to transmission from asymptomatic infections confirms a hypothesis from Nishiura after analysing symptomatic cases occurring post-disembarkation.
source: Our estimated substantial contribution to transmission from asymptomatic infections confirms a hypothesis from Nishiura after analysing symptomatic cases occurring post-disembarkation (Nishiura, 2020).
evidence: The claim compares the study's findings to a previous hypothesis, supported by citation.

claim: The initial reproduction number was 9.3 (7.4–10.6).
source: Our initial reproduction number of 9.3 (7.4–10.6) reflects the high transmission environment expected on cruise ships via increased contacts in a confined space, although lower than the value found in an earlier analysis by Rocklöv et al., 2020.
evidence: The claim is based on model estimates.

claim: The initial reproduction number reflects the high transmission environment expected on cruise ships via increased contacts in a confined space.
source: Our initial reproduction number of 9.3 (7.4–10.6) reflects the high transmission environment expected on cruise ships via increased contacts in a confined space, although lower than the value found in an earlier analysis by Rocklöv et al., 2020.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the model estimate based on knowledge of cruise ship environments.

claim: The finding of similar contribution to transmission from presymptomatic and symptomatic individuals matches findings by others.
source: Our finding of similar contribution to transmission from presymptomatic and symptomatic individuals also matches findings by others (Ganyani et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2020a; He et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim compares the study's findings to other studies, supported by citations.

claim: Having symptoms, or at least being aware of them, is not required in the transmission of SARS-CoV-2.
source: In line with this, it is clear that having symptoms, or at least being aware of them, is not required in the transmission of SARS-CoV-2 (Ganyani et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2020a; He et al., 2020; Kimball et al., 2020; Wei et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: While a cough may increase spread of respiratory infections, it is not a requirement for transmission.
source: Although cough is often considered essential for transmission of respiratory infections (Patterson and Wood, 2019), work in tuberculosis, influenza and other coronaviruses has shown that while a cough may increase spread, it is not a requirement.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation and draws on knowledge from other respiratory infections.

claim: Transmission from breathing, talking and sneezing is possible for SARS-CoV-2.
source: Transmission from breathing, talking and sneezing is also possible, as well as transmission from contaminated surfaces (van Doremalen et al., 2020; Leung et al., 2020; Asadi et al., 2019; Williams et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies on transmission modes.

claim: Transmission from contaminated surfaces is possible for SARS-CoV-2.
source: Transmission from breathing, talking and sneezing is also possible, as well as transmission from contaminated surfaces (van Doremalen et al., 2020; Leung et al., 2020; Asadi et al., 2019; Williams et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies on transmission modes.

claim: On January 20th, the Diamond Princess cruise ship departed from Yokohama on a tour of Southeast Asia.
source: On January 20th, the Diamond Princess cruise ship departed from Yokohama on a tour of Southeast Asia.
evidence: The claim is a factual statement about the timeline of events.

claim: A passenger that disembarked on January 25th in Hong Kong subsequently tested positive for SARS-CoV-2 on February 1st.
source: A passenger that disembarked on January 25th in Hong Kong subsequently tested positive for SARS-CoV-2 on February 1st, reporting the date of symptom onset as January 23rd.
evidence: The claim is a factual statement about the timeline of events.

claim: The passenger who tested positive reported the date of symptom onset as January 23rd.
source: A passenger that disembarked on January 25th in Hong Kong subsequently tested positive for SARS-CoV-2 on February 1st, reporting the date of symptom onset as January 23rd.
evidence: The claim is a factual statement about the timeline of events.

claim: The Diamond Princess began quarantine on February 5th with all passengers confined to their cabins and crew undertaking essential activities only.
source: The ship began quarantine on February 5th with all passengers confined to their cabins and crew undertaking essential activities only.
evidence: The claim is a factual statement about the quarantine measures.

claim: At the start of quarantine there were 3711 individuals on board (2666 passengers and 1045 crew) with a median age of 65 (45–75 interquartile range).
source: At the start of quarantine there were 3711 individuals on board (2666 passengers and 1045 crew) with a median age of 65 (45–75 interquartile range).
evidence: The claim is a factual statement about the population on the ship.

claim: Testing capacity was limited until February 11th and before then the majority of individuals tested had reported symptoms.
source: Testing capacity was limited until February 11th and before then the majority of individuals tested had reported symptoms, referred to here as 'symptom-based testing'.
evidence: The claim is a factual statement about testing practices.

claim: All individuals with a positive test at any stage were promptly removed from the ship and isolated.
source: All individuals with a positive test at any stage were promptly removed from the ship and isolated.
evidence: The claim is a factual statement about the response to positive tests.

claim: After February 11th, testing capacity increased and the testing of individuals irrespective of symptoms was scaled up.
source: After February 11th, testing capacity increased and the testing of individuals irrespective of symptoms, referred to here as 'symptom-agnostic testing', was scaled up.
evidence: The claim is a factual statement about testing practices.

claim: In total, 314 symptomatic and 320 pre- or asymptomatic infections were reported before disembarkation was principally completed on February 21st.
source: In total, 314 symptomatic and 320 pre- or asymptomatic infections were reported before disembarkation was principally completed on February 21st.
evidence: The claim is a factual statement about the number of infections detected.

claim: The model assumed that individuals in the presymptomatic, asymptomatic or symptomatic state test positive and have independent infectiousness, expressed relative to those with symptomatic disease.
source: Individuals in the presymptomatic, asymptomatic or symptomatic state are assumed to test positive and have independent infectiousness, expressed relative to those with symptomatic disease.
evidence: The claim describes a model assumption.

claim: Following exposure, an individual is assumed to test negative for SARS-CoV-2 for the duration of the latent phase.
source: Following exposure, after which an individual is assumed to test negative for SARS-CoV-2 for the duration of the latent phase (see Table 2), a proportion of individuals proceed asymptomatically with the remainder becoming presymptomatic.
evidence: The claim describes a model assumption.

claim: The model assumed a universal probability of becoming either presymptomatic or asymptomatic, independent of who infected whom.
source: This proportion equates to a universal probability of becoming either presymptomatic or asymptomatic, independent of who infected whom.
evidence: The claim describes a model assumption.

claim: Individuals with presymptomatic infection are either detected through symptom-agnostic testing before being removed from the ship, or develop symptomatic disease.
source: Individuals with presymptomatic infection are either detected through symptom-agnostic testing before being removed from the ship, or develop symptomatic disease.
evidence: The claim describes model structure.

claim: Once symptomatic disease starts, individuals can either recover undetected on the ship or be detected through symptom-based testing and removed from the ship with an average delay of one day following symptom onset.
source: Once symptomatic disease starts, individuals can either recover undetected on the ship or, following the start of quarantine on February 5th, be detected through symptom-based testing and removed from the ship with an average delay of one day following symptom onset.
evidence: The claim describes model structure and assumptions.

claim: The model allowed for individuals to test positive after their infectious period for an average of seven days.
source: We allowed for individuals to test positive after their infectious period for an average of seven days (Woelfel et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim describes a model assumption supported by citation.

claim: After seven days post-infectious period, individuals are assumed to test negative.
source: After this, we assume they would test negative.
evidence: The claim describes a model assumption.

claim: Symptom-agnostic testing was assumed to have been random amongst those not reporting symptoms.
source: Symptom-agnostic testing was assumed to have been random amongst those not reporting symptoms and no delay was introduced between testing and removal of those that tested positive from the ship.
evidence: The claim describes a model assumption.

claim: No delay was introduced between testing and removal of those that tested positive from the ship.
source: Symptom-agnostic testing was assumed to have been random amongst those not reporting symptoms and no delay was introduced between testing and removal of those that tested positive from the ship.
evidence: The claim describes a model assumption.

claim: All testing was assumed to have 100% sensitivity and specificity.
source: All testing was assumed to have 100% sensitivity and specificity.
evidence: The claim describes a model assumption.

claim: The between-group contact rate was assumed to be a fixed factor of 1/10th of the within-passenger rate.
source: We estimated the within-crew and within-passenger contact rates through calibration to the data, but assumed that the between-group contact rate was a fixed factor of 1/10th of the within-passenger rate, and explored the impact of this assumption in sensitivity analyses.
evidence: The claim describes a model assumption.

claim: The model assumed that the infectiousness of all transmissible states was constant over time.
source: Our model also assumed that the infectiousness of all transmissible states was constant over time.
evidence: The claim describes a model assumption.

claim: The model assumed that the probability of an individual progressing to either a presymptomatic or asymptomatic infection was independent of who infected whom.
source: A similar simplification was made by assuming that the probability of an individual progressing to either a presymptomatic or asymptomatic infection was independent of who infected whom.
evidence: The claim describes a model assumption.

claim: It is possible that transmission from a symptomatic infection may be more likely to ultimately result in another symptomatic infection, owing to a higher infecting dose.
source: It is possible, however, that transmission from a symptomatic infection may be more likely to ultimately result in another symptomatic infection, owing to a higher infecting dose for example.
evidence: The claim is a speculation about a potential mechanism.

claim: A net reproduction number for presymptomatic passengers at the start of the outbreak of over 20 is unlikely.
source: One can argue that a net reproduction number for presymptomatic passengers at the start of the outbreak of over 20 in this population, as required if asymptomatic individuals are effectively unable to transmit (range for relative infectiousness of 0–1%) is unlikely.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on comparison to known reproduction numbers for other diseases.

claim: Such high reproductive numbers are not usually seen, exceeding for example values found for norovirus outbreaks on cruise ships.
source: Such high reproductive numbers are not usually seen, exceeding for example values found for norovirus outbreaks on cruise ships (Gaythorpe et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation and draws on knowledge of other disease outbreaks.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 has been shown to survive on surfaces.
source: While SARS-CoV-2 has been shown to survive on surfaces (van Doremalen et al., 2020), this does not seem to be the primary mode of transmission.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation.

claim: Surface transmission does not seem to be the primary mode of transmission for SARS-CoV-2.
source: While SARS-CoV-2 has been shown to survive on surfaces (van Doremalen et al., 2020), this does not seem to be the primary mode of transmission.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on current understanding of transmission modes.

claim: There is growing evidence around viral load in asymptomatic infections and their involvement in transmission chains.
source: In combination with growing evidence around viral load in asymptomatic infections and their involvement in transmission chains (Lavezzo et al., 2020), as well as anecdotal evidence about transmission from asymptomatic individuals (Bai et al., 2020; Chau et al., 2020) including in closed populations (Arons et al., 2020), it is reasonable to assume that asymptomatic infections play some role in ongoing SARS-CoV transmission.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies on viral load and transmission.

claim: There is anecdotal evidence about transmission from asymptomatic individuals.
source: In combination with growing evidence around viral load in asymptomatic infections and their involvement in transmission chains (Lavezzo et al., 2020), as well as anecdotal evidence about transmission from asymptomatic individuals (Bai et al., 2020; Chau et al., 2020) including in closed populations (Arons et al., 2020), it is reasonable to assume that asymptomatic infections play some role in ongoing SARS-CoV transmission.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to case reports.

claim: It is reasonable to assume that asymptomatic infections play some role in ongoing SARS-CoV-2 transmission.
source: In combination with growing evidence around viral load in asymptomatic infections and their involvement in transmission chains (Lavezzo et al., 2020), as well as anecdotal evidence about transmission from asymptomatic individuals (Bai et al., 2020; Chau et al., 2020) including in closed populations (Arons et al., 2020), it is reasonable to assume that asymptomatic infections play some role in ongoing SARS-CoV transmission.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on multiple lines of evidence from citations.

claim: In 83% of the scenarios compatible with the data, asymptomatic infections were responsible for more than half of all transmission.
source: In our model, asymptomatic infections were responsible for more than half of all transmission in 83% of the scenarios compatible with the data.
evidence: The claim is based on model analysis.

claim: The conclusion that asymptomatic infections may have contributed substantially to ongoing transmission is critically dependent on the setting.
source: It is important to note that our conclusion that asymptomatic infections may have contributed substantially to ongoing transmission is critically dependent on the setting.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the study's findings emphasizing context-dependence.

claim: Symptomatic infections were quickly identified and removed from the ship before symptom-agnostic testing began, thereby leaving asymptomatic infections to dominate transmission.
source: In this case symptomatic infections were quickly identified and removed from the ship before symptom-agnostic testing began, thereby leaving asymptomatic infections to dominate transmission.
evidence: The claim is an inference about the mechanism explaining the high contribution of asymptomatic infections.

claim: The dominance of asymptomatic infections in transmission should not be interpreted as a constant of nature, but instead an important consideration in settings where prompt isolation of symptomatic infections is already in place.
source: Such dominance should therefore not be interpreted as a constant of nature, but instead an important consideration in settings where prompt isolation of symptomatic infections is already in place but with little to no consideration for asymptomatic infections.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation and inference about the generalizability of the findings.
